summary.text: The gut microbiota is the bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses that live in the digestive tracts of animals.
The gut is the main location of the human microbiome, and the colon holds the densest microbial community studied so far, with 300 to 1000 species.
It affects resistance to pathogens, immune control and the breakdown of food and drugs, and imbalances are associated with diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease.

facts.label: Main location
facts.value: The gut is the main site of the human microbiome

facts.label: Settling in
facts.value: Approaches an adult-like state by age two

items.prompt: After a bowl of bran cereal, what job do some gut microbes do for the person who ate it?

options.label: Stop it from being broken down so it leaves unchanged
Break it down into short-chain fatty acids that the body absorbs
Turn it into stomach acid that kills other bacteria
Absorb it themselves so the body gains nothing from it

items.explain: Some gut microbes ferment dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids, which the host absorbs.

items.prompt: Far fewer microbes live in the stomach than in the colon. What is a main reason?

options.label: Too little food ever reaches it for microbes to feed on
Its walls are too dry for microbes to cling to
Microbes are swept out of it every few minutes
The stomach's high acidity means most microorganisms cannot survive there

items.explain: Most microorganisms cannot survive in the stomach because of its high acidity.

items.prompt: Some gut microbes do more than share space without harming us. What does that make the relationship?

options.label: Mutualistic, since the host gains from what they produce
Commensal, since neither side gains anything
Parasitic, since the microbes gain and the host loses
Pathogenic, since the microbes cause disease

items.explain: The relationship with some gut microbes is not merely commensal but mutualistic, as they ferment fiber into compounds the host absorbs.

items.prompt: Patients with certain illnesses turn out to share an unbalanced mix of gut microbes. What is that imbalance called?

options.label: Enterotype, a classification of the gut ecosystem
Metagenome, the combined genomes of all the gut microbes
Dysbiosis, an imbalance in the microbial community
Commensalism, a coexistence that does no harm

items.explain: Imbalances in the gut microbiota are called dysbiosis and have been associated with numerous diseases.

items.prompt: A man swaps his usual meals for a very different diet. What should researchers expect for his gut microbiota?

options.label: Some of it shifts, since its makeup changes when the diet changes
Nothing at all, because it is fixed at birth
It is wiped out and rebuilt from scratch
Only the fungi change, while the bacteria stay put

items.explain: Gut microbiota composition changes when diet changes, although within a person it stays fairly constant with some alterations from diet, lifestyle and age.

items.prompt: Gut bacteria ferment food and leave products behind. Which group helps process those leftovers?

options.label: Fungi
Archaea
Viruses
Protists

items.explain: Archaea are a large class of gut flora important in the metabolism of the bacterial products of fermentation.

paragraphs.heading: What lives in the gut
paragraphs.text: The gut microbiota is the crowd of microorganisms found in an animal's digestive tract, among them bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses. All of their genomes taken together are called the gastrointestinal metagenome. In people, the gut is the main home of the human microbiome. It holds more bacteria, and more kinds of bacteria, than any other part of the body, roughly 10¹³–10¹⁴, or 10 to 100 trillion.

paragraphs.heading: A map from stomach to colon
paragraphs.text: The mix of microbes changes along the digestive tract. The stomach is so acidic that most microorganisms cannot survive there, and the stomach and small intestine generally hold relatively few bacterial species. The colon is the densest microbial community yet studied in people, with between 300 and 1000 species. Bacteria are the largest and best-studied part: 99% of them come from about 30 or 40 species, and the genus Bacteroides alone makes up about 30%. More than 99% of gut bacteria are anaerobes.

paragraphs.heading: Partners, not just lodgers
paragraphs.text: For some gut microbes, the tie with us goes beyond commensal, meaning harmless living side by side, to a mutualistic relationship. Some break down dietary fiber by fermentation, making short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like acetic acid and butyric acid that the host then absorbs. Gut bacteria also help make certain B vitamins and vitamin K, and process bile acids, sterols and xenobiotics. Their products work across the body somewhat like hormones, and the gut flora itself seems to act like an endocrine organ.

paragraphs.heading: Settling in and staying put
paragraphs.text: In humans the gut flora takes hold at birth and shifts toward an adult-like state by the age of two. That shift happens alongside the maturing of the gut lining and its mucosal barrier, which lets the body live with its microbes while guarding against harmful ones. A few core species are shared by most people, but populations can differ widely. Within one person they stay fairly steady over time, changing somewhat with lifestyle, diet and age.

paragraphs.heading: Effects far beyond digestion
paragraphs.text: The gut microbiota helps resist pathogens, maintains the intestinal lining, processes food and drug compounds and steers immune function. It even affects behavior through the gut–brain axis. Imbalances, called dysbiosis, have been linked to inflammatory bowel disease, certain cancers and even neurological disorders, which has spurred work on therapies aimed at the microbiome. Disturbed gut flora has also been connected with many inflammatory and autoimmune conditions.

paragraphs.heading: Much still unknown
paragraphs.text: Fungi, protists, archaea and viruses also live in the gut, but less is known about what they do. Many gut species have never been studied outside their hosts because they cannot be cultured. The gut microbiota is estimated to carry about a hundred times as many genes as the human genome. Industrialization is linked to changes in these communities, and lost diversity could drive some species extinct; in 2018 researchers proposed a biobank to store human microbiota.
